'''''Eucalyptus gunnii''''', commonly known as '''cider gum''',<ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus gunnii'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20gunnii |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=24 July 2019}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Myrtaceae]]. It is a small to medium-sized tree with mostly smooth bark, lance-shaped to egg-shaped adult leaves, flower buds in groups of three, white flowers and cylindrical to barrel-shaped fruit.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus gunnii'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of up to {{cvt|25|m}} and has smooth bark, or mottled white or grey bark, sometimes with persistent rough bark on the up to {{cvt|1|m}} on the lowest part of the trunk. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] leaves arranged in opposite pairs. Juvenile stems can be rounded or square in cross section,<ref>{{Cite web|title=''Eucalyptus gunnii''|url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_gunnii.htm|access-date=2021-12-11|website=apps.lucidcentral.org}}</ref> with a [[lignotuber]]. The juvenile leaves are heart-shaped to more or less round, greyish green or [[wikt:glaucous#Adjective|glaucous]], {{cvt|13-45|mm}} long and {{cvt|17-40|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, lance-shaped to egg-shaped, the same dull greyish to bluish green on both sides, {{cvt|40-90|mm}} long and {{cvt|12-35|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|9-23|mm}} long.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus gunnii'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_gunnii.htm |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=13 June 2025}}</ref><ref name="Brooker">{{cite book |last1=Brooker |first1=Murray I.H. (Ian) |last2=Kleinig |first2=David A. |title=''Eucalyptus'' - an in illustrated guide to identification |date=1996 |publisher=Reed Books |location=Melbourne |isbn=978-1-876334-36-9 |page=136}}</ref><ref name="Kelly">{{cite book |last1=Kelly |first1=Stan |title=''Eucalypts'' |volume=2 |date=1983 |publisher=Thomas Nelson |location=Melbourne, Victory. |isbn=0-17-006222-8 |page=29}}</ref>

The flowers are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of three on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|3-9|mm}} long, the individual buds sessile or on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|4|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval, {{cvt|5-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with a conical, rounded or flattened [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. It flowers in most months and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody cylindrical to barrel-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|5-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-7|mm}} wide with the valves near rim level or enclosed.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="Brooker" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus gunnii'' was first formally described in 1844 by the British botanist [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]] in the ''London Journal of Botany''. The [[Type (biology)|type]] material was collected "on the elevated tablelands of the interior of Tasmania, especially in the neighborhood of the lakes" by [[Ronald Campbell Gunn]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus gunnii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455087 |publisher=APNI|access-date=23 July 2019}}</ref><ref name="Hook.f.">{{cite journal |last1=Hooker |first1=Joseph Dalton |editor-last1=Hooker |editor-first1=William Jackson |title=Note of the Cider Tree |journal=London Journal of Botany |date=1844 |volume=3 |pages=499–501 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/6314#page/503/mode/1up |access-date=24 July 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] honours the collector of the type material.<ref name="CANBR" />

[[Joseph Maiden]]'s 1889 book ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia''<nowiki />' recorded that common names in Tasmania are "cider gum" and in southeastern Australia occasionally as the "sugar gum" and that in the same part it is known as "white gum", "swamp gum" or "white swamp gum". In the [[Old Noarlunga, South Australia|Noarlunga]] and [[Rapid Bay]] districts of [[South Australia]] it is known as "bastard white gum", occasionally as "yellow gum." Near [[Bombala, New South Wales]] two varieties go by the names of "flooded or bastard gum" and "red gum", although the species only occurs in Tasmania.<ref name="Maiden">{{cite book |last1=Maiden |first1=Joseph |title=The useful native plants of Australia (including Tasmania) |date=1889 |volume=1889 |publisher=Turner and Henderson |location=Sydney |page=27 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/45057#page/45/mode/1up |access-date=24 July 2019}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Cider gum is native to woodland in Tasmania, where it occurs on the plains and slopes of the [[Central Highlands (Tasmania)|central plateaux]] and [[dolerite]] mountains at altitudes up to about {{cvt|1100|m}}, with isolated occurrences south of Hobart.<ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="Pandani">{{cite book |last1=Kirkpatrick |first1=James Barrie |last2=Backhouse |first2=Sue |title=''Native Trees of Tasmania'' |date=1985 |page=98 |isbn=0-646-43088-2 |publisher=Pandani Press |location=Hobart}}</ref><ref name=brooker>Brooker, K. (1996). ''Eucalyptus. An illustrated guide to identification''. Reed Books, Melbourne</ref> It grows in higher altitudes where the summers are mild and winters cold with many frost and heavy snow, and annual average rainfall is about {{cvt|1800|mm}}.<ref name="Kelly" />

This species of eucalypt has been introduced to New Zealand and parts of the Caucasus.<ref name=powo>{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online |title=''Eucalyptus gunnii'' Hook.f. |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:592987-1 |access-date=1 April 2023 }}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==
This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web 
| title=''Eucalyptus gunnii'' AGM | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/6888/Eucalyptus-gunnii/Details
| publisher=Royal Horticultural Society | access-date=19 June 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 37 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 18 February 2018}}</ref> This species is noted for exceptional cold tolerance for a eucalyptus (to −14 °C, exceptionally −20 °C for brief periods) and is now commonly planted as an [[ornamental tree]] across the British Isles.<ref name="CSIRO">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=Murray Ian Hill (Ian) |title=A Key to Eucalypts in Britain and Ireland |url=https://cdn.forestresearch.gov.uk/1983/03/fcbk050.pdf |publisher=CSIRO; Division of Forest Research |access-date=13 June 2025}}</ref>

The fragrant leaves give off [[essential oil]]s when they are creased or burned, which are used in different forms (floral composition, [[infusion]], [[tincture]], oil, etc) to treat many [[respiratory disease]]s, [[rheumatism]], [[migraine]]s, [[fatigue]] and as [[antiseptic]].<ref name="Tree">{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=Owen |last2=More |first2=David |title=Tree Guide: The Most Complete Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Europe |date=2004 |publisher=Collins |isbn=978-84-282-1400-1}}</ref>

The [[Aboriginal Tasmanians|Aboriginal people of Tasmania]] used the sap of the tree to produce a [[fermented beverage]] called ''way-a-linah''.<ref name="nature">{{cite journal |last1=Varela |first1=Cristian |last2=Sundstrom |first2=Joanna |last3=Cuijvers |first3=Kathleen |last4=Jiranek |first4=Vladimir |last5=Borneman |first5=Anthony |title=Discovering the indigenous microbial communities associated with the natural fermentation of sap from the cider gum ''Eucalyptus gunnii'' |journal=Scientific Reports |date=December 2020 |volume=10 |issue=1 |page=14716 |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-71663-x |doi-access=free|pmid=32895409 |pmc=7477236 |bibcode=2020NatSR..1014716V |s2cid=221536063 }}</ref>
